Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: fact-checked peer-reviewed publication trusted source proofread The GIST Add to Preferred Sources Credit: Unsplash/CC0 Public Domain In 2021, Texas suffered the worst energy infrastructure failure in state history, following three severe winter storms in February. At least 246 people were killed as a result of the disruptions, which led to food, water, heat and electricity shortages. If energy officials had had more time to prepare for the storms, for example by bringing in more trucks of natural gas to disrupted areas, damage from the event could have been mitigated. Unfortunately, weather forecasts beyond two weeks are notoriously unreliable, making for a tighter window for energy operators, farmers and emergency response officials around the globe. A new technique by a team including researchers at MIT significantly improves weather forecasting beyond two weeks. The researchers developed a machine-learning model that learns to correct errors in existing forecasting models to improve their output over the two-to-six-week time frame. When applied to a gold-standard forecasting model, it doubled forecasting accuracy over that time frame, placing first in a prominent international forecasting competition. In a new paper in Nature , the researchers describe their approach and show how it enables forecasts that for the first time beat climatologic averages between two and six weeks. "Not only does this do better on time-averaged forecasts for this range, which is already very useful for farmers and members of the energy industry trying to match supply with demand, but it also improves predictions of extreme weather events, whether it's flooding or cold spells or something else," co-author and MIT research scientist Judah Cohen says. "It's really important to predict both, but extreme events might be the most impactful part of this for society." Joining Cohen on the paper are lead authors Hannah Guan, a Harvard College undergraduate; Soukayna Mouatadid, a University of Toronto postdoc; Genevieve Flaspohler SM '18, Ph.D. '22; Paulo Orenstein, an associate professor at Brazil's National Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics; Jeremy Berman of the data company DTN; Jakob Schloer and Joshua Talib, researchers with the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts; and Alex Lu, Haiyu Dong, Jonathan Weyn, Zekun Ni and Lester Mackey, all researchers at Microsoft. Longer forecasts In the 1970s, longtime MIT professor Edward Lorenz came up with the idea of chaos theory to describe how tiny changes in initial weather conditions lead to completely different outcomes. "He came up with this theoretical two-week limit where beyond that, we just can't predict weather because the noise in the system grows so much that it overwhelms any signal you start with," Cohen says. "That had a strong influence on the field that may have held people back from exploring forecasting beyond the two-week range. I never really believed that completely. "In theory the atmosphere can create an infinite number of patterns, but it likes to fall into these favorite patterns over and over again. Once one thing happens, I think you can predict the domino that will fall after that, and the domino that will fall after that." Today, the best weather forecasts come from either dynamical models , which numerically simulate how the atmosphere and oceans evolve over time, or artificial intelligence models, which learn to make predictions from historical weather data. AI models have shown improvements in predicting weather at short ranges, but they're even worse than dynamical models at longer time ranges. Subscribe Cohen, who is based in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, focuses on forecasting weather two to six weeks in advance, which is known as subseasonal forecasting. "That range is referred to as the 'predictability desert,' because in the short range you can capitalize on the initial conditions in the climate system and the atmosphere, and on the longer term you have these slow, varying boundary forces, like the super El Niño everyone's focused on this winter," Cohen says. "The subseasonal range can't take advantage of either of those. In most cases forecasting in the subseasonal ranges is no different than going to a casino and rolling the dice." Cohen credits his co-author Mackey, whom he has been collaborating with for more than a decade, with the initial idea of using machine learning to reduce errors in forecasting models. "We built this wrapper—Lester calls it postprocessing," Cohen says. "We know AI models have a lot of errors, so we thought maybe we can quantify those errors and remove them."
